requirements.text: Track the movement of lapsed quantities in an area, including: Which permit and well obtained the lapsed quantities. Where the lapsed quantities are located. Why the quantities are lapsed (i.e. expired, cancelled, retired). What MFL zone the lapsed quantities are in.
Track the relocation of active water use within the SWUCA.
Report on the history of irrigation water conserving credits, including the balance, how much earned, and how much used, and drought quantities.
Track and report on the history of permitted data, such as use type, irrigated acres, and pumpage (one use would be to know whether expired permits have had quantities reallocated).

Track and measure alternative source projects: Surface water or stormwater projects. Reclaimed water (reuse water). Augmented surface water (reservoirs, harvesting of high flows (floodwaters). ASR (Aquifer storage recovery). Desalination. Conservation.
View the spatial impact of a person's application with other active applications on-line so the applicant or evaluator has a visual of who else is available to compete for quantities with.
Create heat map indicating who was over-pumping, who was not over-pumping, or who was using their water credits.
Report on the permits that have been relocated by a permit holder.
Track the impact that water use has to the set MFL levels.
Track net benefit changes.
Report the net benefit amount in MGD for: Change of permitted location or use, Land use change, Use of lapsed quantities, Water withdrawal credit (replacement, reclaimed water).
Mark those permits that have a land use change so the quantities can be relocated to the public supply utility.
Create layer that includes "cones of depression" for the MFL information, which will indicate the area of influence to an MFL.
Report on any water use amounts sold or given from one permit to another permit, especially reclaimed water.
For mitigation of MFL impacts, report on the improvement percentage amount, where it was located, the cost, how the decrease was obtained and what impacts it had.
Report on how much water was made available through the District's water resource development projects.
Report on the permit duration.
Should allow comparison to adjacent districts GIS layers to permit GIS layer to access adjacent data.
Report compliance on a permit (not wells).
Report on competing applications (including ones that are in modification or expiring).
Supply the Regulatory requirements of MFL data.
Be able to determine the availability of alternative use supplies, such as reclaimed water and desalination.
Report the Reservation from use amounts allocated to certain participants.
Track ownership of wells or permits over the life of the withdrawal point so the relocated quantities can be traced from owner to owner.
Be able to look at permitted quantities, actual quantities (pumpage), and the resources it uses (Water Management DB).
Ability to track requested and permitted quantities.
Identify when a standby permit is reactivated due to the loss of alternative quantities.
Have a heat map that shows permit information for specific time periods.

Ability for public utilities and internal staff to find existing permits in or near their service area so they can spatially see what water is available, or may become available, when they plan for their future growth and water resources.
Analyze permits using a soils type GIS layer.
Ability to have printable and customizable maps.
Identify when the District or another governmental agency purchases land, a link should be available to show if there is a permit on that area so it can be retired.
Need to know how water use changes when land use changes.

Have an easy way to query data by various fields: Issue date, Expiration date, Use type or other commodity, Predominate use, Pumpage reports, Permitted quantities, Permit status (active/delete/app/permit).
Ability to pull a well package that provides a view of water use at a particular time that is then plugged into models used to generate water use amounts.
The ability to associate permitted quantities, pumpage quantities, and use code data at the well level.
Track changes in land use and how it affects water availability.
Need historical data for Water Use Permits including their spatial representations (polygons).
Must be able to track trends in land use and water use changes.
Ability to track water use over time and negotiate reasonable new water use based on water use pumpage trends.
Track by withdrawal source – what aquifer or USGS water body are general and Individual permits pumping from.
Have map be able to show quantity of pumpage.
Provide the ability for applicants or District staff to compare the percentage a permit is over-pumping, based on use type, against the regional average for the same use type.
Need to know what aquifer is being pumped from.
Select water use data temporally or with geographic overlays, which can be from another layer or graphics on the page.
Select water use based on predominant use, use types, and regions they fall in.
Generate monthly reports for Board Packet that shows the difference in quantities permitted every month for specified geographic areas.
Establish relationships between inputs (i.e. rainfall) and pumpage data.
Show the intensity of water use in a geographic area on a color-coded map.
Identify different types of water use, such as groundwater, surface water, and re-use.
Know how much water has been permitted and how much has been used based on land use over time.
Support extraction or reporting of data for ad-hoc geographic areas by using spatial queries such as graphics or polygon buffering.
Track aquifer level changes, lake level changes, rainfall level changes, and stream flow changes by area over time.
Create layer that shows the Developments of Regional Impacts (DRI) and their status.
Identify what lakes are stressed, when they became stressed, and if/when they came off stressed list.
Track pumpage oddities.
Track permittees not submitting conditional/pumpage reports, and generate a map showing their locations.
Obtain report of those out of compliance of permit conditions by over-pumping their allowable quantities.

Need a protocol to assess how the actual flow and levels (AFL) compare to the established minimum flows and levels (MFL), including general trending information and whether waterbody-specific criteria are being met.
Use system to publish a chart or graph that compares the MFL to a running average of AFL's.
Ability to add estimated quantities for unmetered permits, which is found in the Water Estimates Database.
Provide access to population data in system that are aggregated to appropriate geographic areas.
The ability to access crop report information spatially and temporally.
Link between Water Use Permits (WUP), Environmental Resource Permits (ERP), and Well Construction Permits.
The system shall implement role-based access control (RBAC) to restrict access to sensitive permit documents and legal records based on the user's authorized role and department.
The system shall implement centralized authentication, enforce secure session timeouts, and maintain an immutable audit log of all access and modifications to sensitive permit and water use data.
The system shall render map views and generate standard reports within 5 seconds for 95% of requests under normal load.
The system shall implement automated data integrity checks for all imported datasets, with a maximum allowable data discrepancy rate of 0.1% for automated transfers.

Define specific performance metrics, such as: 'The system shall render map layers within 3 seconds for 95% of requests and generate standard reports within 10 seconds for datasets up to 100,000 records.'

Replace with a concrete NFR: 'The web-based interface shall provide a visual indicator for processes exceeding 2 seconds and complete all standard UI interactions within 500ms under normal network conditions.'

OPEN: The PRD lacks requirements for data encryption, both for data at rest in the databases and data in transit across the network. - All sensitive water use and permit data shall be encrypted at rest using industry-standard algorithms, and all data in transit between servers and clients shall be encrypted using TLS 1.2 or higher.

OPEN: The PRD does not define the expected concurrent user load or data volume growth, which is critical for an architecture-centric project. - The system shall support at least 50 concurrent users and a data growth rate of 10% per annum without degradation of performance metrics.

OPEN: The PRD mentions 'Backup and Recovery' as a topic for the Architecture Document but provides no RTO (Recovery Time Objective) or RPO (Recovery Point Objective) requirements. - The system shall have an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 24 hours for all critical databases.

OPEN: The PRD lacks information regarding the expected concurrent user load or the total volume of data (number of permits, wells, and historical records) the system must support. - Include a section in the Supplementary Specification defining the expected peak concurrent users (e.g., 50 users) and the total data volume (e.g., 50,000 permits, 200,000 wells) to guide architectural design.
